EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The Cooperation Framework between the United Nations and the Government of Serbia for 2026–2030 (CF)
is the primary tool for analysing, planning and implementing UN development activities at the country level
in alignment with the 2030 Agenda. It outlines the contributions of the UN system to the Sustainable
Development Goals (SDGs) and national development priorities, including European Union (EU) accession.
The CF reflects the UN’s comparative advantage and is aligned with the principles of leaving no one behind
(LNOB), human rights, gender equality and women’s empowerment and internationalstandards and treaties.
The CF is based on the development challenges identified in the UN Country Analysis (CA), the national
development priorities, including EU accession, and lessons learned from the previous Cooperation
Framework (2021–2025). The CF supports Serbia’s aspiration to achieve the 2030 Agenda and complete its
EU accession process, ensuring alignment with the country’s broader reform objectives. It is based on
extensive consultations with key stakeholders from the government, non-government organizations, media,
academia and private sector throughout different stages in its development.
Serbia is an upper middle-income and high human development country in Southeast Europe, sharing
borders with eight other countries. Under UN Security Council Resolution 1244 (1999), an international civil
and security presence has been established in Kosovo1,specifically the United NationsInterim Administration
Mission in Kosovo (UNMIK) and the Kosovo Force (KFOR). The work of the UN Team supporting the
implementation of Sustainable Development Goalsis carried out as part of continuing UNMIK mandate under
the authority of UN Security Council Resolution 1244 (1999). It is the largest and among the fastest growing
economies in the region, likely to reach high-income status in the next decade. Serbia has made significant
progress in achieving the SDGs notably in health, education and social protection and improving the living
conditions of its people particularly its children, and is a leader in digital transformation. A stable geo-political
situation in the region and beyond is an important prerequisite of peace and development in the country.
Serbia is undergoing a rapid demographic transition, characterized by an ageing population, declining fertility
rates and significant out-migration, resulting in an 8.5% reduction in total population over the past 12 years.
The housing sector faces significant challenges, marked by a limited supply of affordable and adequate
housing, particularly for vulnerable populations. Additionally, the country faces environmental challenges,
including heavy reliance on fossil fuels, biodiversity loss, air and water pollution, unsustainable management
of natural and cultural resources, and increasing vulnerability to climate change, all of which have significant
implications for public health and the economy. Current economic growth trends present a significant
opportunity to accelerate convergence with European living standards. Targeted efforts to address labour
market gaps, align skills with market needs, boost productivity and innovation, and streamline administrative
processes can unlock substantial growth potential over the next two decades.
The country has a progressive constitution that enshrinesfundamental freedoms. Its national laws are largely
compliant with the EU and international norms and standards. Serbia has recently strengthened the legal
framework in a number of areas. There is scope for strengthening the implementation of these through the
further development of supporting instruments and enhanced institutional capacity. Continued efforts to
improve accountability and address perceptions of corruption can build public trust, while promoting
inclusive governance offers a valuable opportunity to expand civic space, advance gender equality, and
ensure stronger protection for human rights defenders and activists.
Serbia lacks a Development Plan that should represent the hierarchically highest long-term document of
development planning. Under the Law on the Planning System (2018) the government was entrusted with
the authority to submit the draft Development Plan to the National Assembly for adoption. Although the
1 All references to Kosovo shall be understood to be in the context of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1244 (1999)3
Development Plan of the Republic of Serbia has not yet been adopted, most planning documents in the
country are aligned with the SDGs. According to data from 2024, the alignment of the goals and sub-goals of
sustainable development with the objectives of the planning framework of the Republic of Serbia amounted
to 79.9%,while in 2023 it stood at 82.7%, and at 78% in 2022. In all stages of drafting legislative acts and
planning documents, the LNOB principle has been introduced, ensuring the inclusion of issues concerning
marginalized groups in the policymaking process.
Serbia is formally committed to the 2030 Agenda and responsibility for oversight and coordination of its
implementation was entrusted to an Inter-Ministerial Working Group, re-established by a Government
decision on 20 December 2024. EU accession is a top national priority and a key driver of sustainable
development. By 2026, the country aims to become fully aligned with EU standards even as the process of
full membership continues. The CF is predicated on the high complementarity between the EU accession and
SDG progress.
The Theory of Change for the CF in Serbia is grounded in the development challenges identified in the CA.
Using systemic enablers such as political commitment to EU integration, stable economic and geopolitical
context, and effective coordination among UN, government and development partners, the CF focuses on
three interdependent strategic priority areas coupled with cross-cutting drivers with lenses on where
progress towards the 2030 Agenda remains insufficient and where the UN can add value. The CF envisions
that: (1) If Serbia rapidly transitions to a gender-responsive, green and digital economy with inclusive access
to opportunities, particularly improving labour market inclusivity by increasing workforce participation
among women, ethnic minorities and youth, addressing skills mismatch, and leveraging the ‘silver economy’,
then its economy will be more sustainable, competitive and inclusive; (2) If demographic shifts are met in a
rights-based and gender-sensitive manner through policies and investments in high-quality, inclusive and
innovative health, education and social protection systems, then well-being will improve for all, especially
women and children; (3) If democratic institutions are strengthened through transparent governance, human
rights protection and civic engagement, particularly for women, then Serbia will build an inclusive,
participatory and cohesive society grounded in rule of law and gender equality; and (4) If these priorities are
supported by the EU accession process, digital transformation, building resilience to shocks, risks and
uncertainties, and strong partnerships and coordination, then Serbia will progress towards the 2030 Agenda
leaving no one behind.
Building on the Theory of Change elaborated above, the UN Country Team (UNCT) in Serbia, in consultation
with key stakeholders, identified three Strategic Priorities and four Outcomes, as follows:
SP 1: Low-carbon, inclusive and resilient growth
Outcome 1: By 2030, sustainable, nature-positive, participatory, accountable, and gender-responsive
solutions for environmental protection, climate and disaster resilience, pollution reduction and the
management of natural and cultural resources — leveraging new technologies and traditional knowledge —
are promoted and implemented.
Outcome 2: By 2030, the economy of Serbia is more sustainable, knowledge-based, competitive and genderresponsive with equitable access to green and digital economic opportunities and SDGs-aligned investment
and financing.
SP 2: Human capital and well-being
Outcome 3: By 2030, all people in Serbia, particularly vulnerable groups, benefit from high-quality, genderresponsive, equitable and inclusive, and innovative health, education and social protection systems, ensuring
well-being across the lifecycle.4
SP 3: Rule of law, human rights, human security and accountable institutions
Outcome 4: By 2030, Serbia ensures an independent and transparent judicial and law enforcement system,
good governance and inclusive digital transformation, civic engagement and full realization of human rights
and gender equality, fostering social cohesion and an inclusive and participatory democracy for all.
Working in partnership with, and leveraging the work of other stakeholders, the UNCT in Serbia will
contribute to the achievement of these strategic priorities and outcomes through technical assistance,
capacity development, innovative pilot initiatives, policy advice, partnerships, mobilization of financial
resources for a transition to a more just, sustainable and resilient economy, and social mobilization, among
others. The UNCT reviewed its configuration, including business models and capacities of contributing UN
entities, to align itself with the CF for effective delivery of results. By leveraging its expertise, and working
together, the UNCT will contribute to accelerated SDG progress through evidence-based approaches,
strategic foresight, innovation and digital transformation, with a focus on behavioural aspects to bring about
the desired changes. It will build on its normative mandate, notably gender equality, women’s empowerment
and ‘leaving no one behind’, as the central approach to this CF.
Implementation of the CF is based on the principle of partnership with the relevant authorities of Serbia. In
order to ensure coherence and effectiveness, implementation will take place through a coordinated
approach, entrusted to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of European Integration, through the
mechanism of the Joint National Steering Committee. The CF will be operationalized through the Joint Work
Plans and monitored through the Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning Plan, which will be prepared for the
entire duration of the CF and periodically reviewed. The legal relationship between the UN and the
Government of Serbia will be governed in line with the legal annex to the CF (Annex 2). Implementation of
the CF will be supported by the Results Groups, Thematic Working Groups and UN Programme Support
Groups and be guided by the UNCT. The CF will undergo a mandatory final independent evaluation in the
penultimate year.

CHAPTER 1: COUNTRY PROGRESS TOWARDS AGENDA 2030
1.1 Country context
Serbia is an upper middle-income country that has achieved sustained economic growth and maintained
macroeconomic stability over the past decade. Its economy is largely service-based with declining shares of
manufacturing and agriculture. The Human Development Report 2025 classified Serbia as a very high human
development country with a Human Development Index (HDI) value of 0.833, ranking 62nd out of 193
countries. Implementation of the 2030 Agenda presents areas of success and some areas where substantial
efforts are needed to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030. The country is making
progress in reducing the share of the population at risk of poverty. Health outcomes and life expectancy are
gradually improving but fall short of European Union (EU) averages. Serbia’s social protection system is a
cornerstone for reducing poverty and inequality. Yet, inequalities persist notably among different ethnic
groups and between rural and urban areas. When adjusted for inequalities, the HDI drops to 0.772, or by
7.3%. In the Global Gender Gap Index 2024, Serbia ranks 26th out of 146 countries, performing very well with
regard to education, health and survival, but with gaps to be filled in terms of labour participation.
The country is facing a rapid demographic transition due to low fertility and out-migration (though it is
becoming increasingly attractive to labour migrants). As a result, Serbia has experienced a shrinkage in the
total population of 8.5% over the past 12 years and an increase in the proportion older than 65 years. Unless
managed proactively, the transition risks putting additional strain on the social protection, health and
pension systems, while threatening economic prosperity with business increasingly finding it difficult to
secure the skills it needs from the labour market. Moreover, the country’s social housing system is
underdeveloped, with public rental housing comprising just 0.5% of the total stock, mainly in the cities. This
scarcity leads to overcrowding and inadequate conditions, especially for low-income and marginalized
groups. While EU- and United Nations (UN)-supported initiatives have provided housing for vulnerable
families, efforts remain fragmented.
Non-communicable diseases (NCDs)—primarily cardiovascular diseases, cancers, respiratory diseases and
diabetes—are the leading public health burden in Serbia, accounting for 94% of all deaths (with nearly 20%
occurring under the age of 60). Mortality rates for preventable cancers such as cervical cancer far exceed EU
averages. Unhealthy lifestyles, marked by high tobacco consumption, further exacerbate the trends, placing
increasing strain on the health system through rising mortality, preventable disease and escalating
healthcare costs. Mental health is also emerging as a health challenge, especially among the young.
Serbia continues to face numerous environmental challenges, including those arising from the share of fossil
fuels in the energy mix, pressures on biodiversity, and various potential forms of pollution affecting air, soil
and water. In addition, the management of natural and cultural resources requires further improvement,
while climate change poses increasing risks. These issues can have a significant impact on public health and
economic development.
The energy sector is undergoing transformation with significant strides being taken towards a cleaner future.
The Government is currently formulating a concrete plan to phase down coal-based power plants, which still
provide more than 65% of Serbia’s energy needs. Air pollution remains a major environmental and public
health challenge, primarily driven by fossil fuel use, inefficient heating and industrial emissions. The
environmental legal and policy framework has shown improvement, aligning increasingly with EU standards,
though implementation is lagging behind as capacities for enforcement remain limited.
The country has a progressive constitution that enshrines fundamental freedoms. Its national laws, covering
various aspects of governance, human rights and economic regulation, are largely compliant with the EU and
international norms and standards. Serbia also has a well-developed legal and institutional framework for
national minority rights, recognized by the Council of Europe as exceeding average European standards.7
However, strengthening judicial independence and enhancing efficiency and capacities of independent
institutions is an area where further progress is needed. Civic space in Serbia is protected by a relatively
strong constitutional and legal framework. The legal framework for media is strong but implementation of
safeguard mechanisms appears insufficient. Disinformation and divisive rhetoric affect the media scene.
Serbia ranks 96th out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) Global Freedom of Press Index
2025. Freedom of assembly in the country is well-protected, including during citizen protests.
Serbia recently strengthened the legal framework for tackling corruption, gender-based violence (GBV),
discrimination, hate crime, human trafficking and gender inequality,
2 with the establishment of the first
ministry in charge of gender equality in the region, ensuring freedom of assembly and participation, safety
of journalists and human rights defenders, and accountability for past human rights violations, among others.
Despite solid legal frameworksin key areas, certain gaps between legal promises and implementation persist.
Accession negotiations with the EU were opened in January 2014, and progress in adoption and
implementation of the EU acquis communautaire is progressing, albeit at a pace that remains below
expectations. To date, 22 out of 35 chapters have been opened, including all those under Cluster 1
(Fundamentals) and Cluster 4 (Green Agenda and Sustainable Connectivity), with two chapters provisionally
closed. In October 2024, the European Commission approved the Reform Agenda for Serbia, facilitating
access to support under the Reform and Growth Facility. EU accession is a key driver of sustainable
development given its strong correlation with SDG progress. By 2026, Serbia aims to become fully compliant
with EU standards even as the process of full membership continues. The Cooperation Framework (CF) is
designed to support and complement these processes, ensuring alignment with national priorities and
Serbia’s broader reform aspirations.
In accordance with the Stabilization and Association Agreement, in 2013, Serbia adopted the first National
Programme for the Adoption of the EU Acquis (NPAA). This document represents a comprehensive plan
encompassing measures, activities and timelines aimed at achieving full alignment with the requirements of
the acquis. This includes its proper transposition into the national legislation and its implementation and
effective and efficient enforcement through an appropriate institutional framework. The first NPAA has been
revised five times so far, in accordance with the various phases and evolving needs of the process. Currently,
the NPAA for the period 2024–2027 is in force.
In addition, the Plan for Fulfilling the Key Obligations in the EU Accession Negotiation Process of the Republic
of Serbia by the end of 2026 has been adopted as a political and operational instrument to guide the
fulfilment of the most important commitments in the negotiation process by the end of 2026. Government
adopted the Plan in April 2025. The document elaborates in detail the key activities required to meet the
benchmarks under each negotiation chapter (except for Chapters 23 - Judiciary and Fundamental Rights, 24
- Justice, Freedom and Security, 34 – Institutions, and 35 – Other Issues for which a specific approach is
applied), including priority legislative initiatives. For the purpose of aligning the NPАA 2024–2027 with the
Plan, the Government of Serbia adopted amendments to the NPАA 2024–2027 in August 2025, with the aim
of taking into account the accelerated dynamics required for fulfilling the key obligations under the
negotiation process by the end of 2026.
1.2 Progress towards Agenda 2030 and the SDGs
Serbia is formally committed to the 2030 Agenda and set up an Inter-Ministerial Working Group in December
2024 with the Minister of Science, Technological Development and Innovation as the chair, responsible for
overseeing and coordinating the 2030 Agenda. The Government has initiated the process of (a) nationalizing
the SDG indicators, (b) aligning SDG implementation with economic,social and other development conditions
2 The Gender Equality Law, adopted in 2021, has been undergoing revision by the Constitutional Court since June 2024, with a review
of its constitutionality, particularly with regard to the provisions on gender-sensitive language.8
in the country, as well as with EU benchmarks, in close coordination with the Statistical Office of the Republic
of Serbia (SORS), and (c) developing the Second Voluntary National Review (VNR).
In September 2024, the President of Serbia attended the Summit of the Future and expressed support for
the Pact for the Future. During the SDG Summit in 2023, Serbia was one of the 40 countries that renewed its
commitments to realizing the 2030 Agenda, while emphasizing the priority of the ‘leave no one behind’
(LNOB) principle in the formulation of public policies. Serbia prepared its first VNR in 2019, presenting it to
the High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development. The country prepares annual statistical reports
on advances made towards the SDGs.
SORS is responsible for monitoring and reporting on progress made by Serbia towards the SDGs. With the
support of the UN Country Team (UNCT) and development partners, and through active collaboration with
Eurostat, it has established a robust SDG monitoring framework containing 159 indicators, 64% of the total
number. The country’s progress towards the SDGs compares favourably with global averages. Among the
SDG indicators being measured at the national level, more than 50% have either been achieved or are
progressing positively. Serbia ranked 35th worldwide, with a score of 77, in the 2024 Sustainable Development
Solutions Network Report, which measures overall progress towards the 17 SDGs.
With regard to the Progress Report on Implementation of the SDGs for 2024, the Republic has made
significant progress, summarised as follows:
PEOPLE [SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5]: Significant progress has been made in reducing the proportion of people
living below the international poverty line (1.1.1) and national poverty line (1.2.1), and those living in
multidimensional poverty (1.2.2). One area of concern is a decline in the total spending on health, education
and social protection as a proportion of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) (1.a.2) [SDG 1]. Prevalence of
moderate or severe food insecurity based on the Food Insecurity Experience Scale (2.1.2) is an area where
progress is higher with targets on maternal mortality ratio (3.1.1), under-five mortality rate (3.2.1) and
neonatal mortality rate (3.2.2) having already been achieved with significant progress made in the areas of
tuberculosisincidence (3.3.2), mortality due to NCDs(3.4.1), death due to road traffic accident injuries(3.6.1)
and out-of-pocket expenses on health as a share of total household expenditure (3.8.2). Yet, adolescent birth
rates are an area of stagnant progress (3.7.2) [SDG 3]. Participation of youth and adults in formal and nonformal education and training hasshown progress(4.3.1) but progressin the participation rate in pre-primary
organized learning is stagnant (4.2.2) [SDG 4]. Serbia has achieved the target of laws and regulations that
guarantee full and equal access by women and men to reproductive healthcare, education and information
(5.6.2) and while significant progress has been made with regard to the proportion of women in managerial
positions (5.5.2), one area of concern is the proportion of seats held by women in the national parliament
and local governments (5.5.1) [SDG 5].
PROSPERITY [SDGs 7, 8, 9 and 10]: The target of the proportion of the population with access to electricity
has been achieved (7.1.1) and significant progress is reported for the share of renewable energy in total
energy consumption (7.2.1) and energy intensity per unit of GDP (7.3.1) [SDG 7]. Significant progress is
reported in the areas of the proportion of informal employment in total employment (8.3.1), average hourly
earnings (8.5.1), unemployment rate (8.5.2) and proportion of youth NEET (8.6.1). Areas of concern include
annual growth rate of real GDP per capita (8.1.1) and domestic material consumption per capita and per unit
of GDP (8.4.2 and 12.2.2) [SDG 8]. Significant progress is reported in passenger and freight volumes (9.1.2),
the proportion of small-scale industries in total industry value added (9.3.1), and research and development
expenditure as a proportion of GDP (9.5.1), while progress in manufacturing employment as a proportion of
total employment (9.2.2) is off-track [SDG 9]. Significant progress has been made in reducing inequalities as
indicated by growth rates in household expenditure as a proportion of the income per capita among the
bottom 40% of the population (10.1.1), proportion of people living below 50% of median income (10.2.1),
the labour share of GDP (10.4.1) and total resource flows for development (10.b.1) [SDG 10].9
PLANET [SDGs 6, 11, 12, 13 and 15]: Serbia has made significant progress in the safe treatment of domestic
and industrial wastewater (6.3.1), water use efficiency (6.4.1) and reduction in level of water stress (6.4.2.).
One area where progress isstagnant isthe proportion of the population using safely managed drinking water
services (6.1.1) [SDG 6]. Data on sustainable cities and communities is scant. Based on available data, the
country has achieved the goal of having a national urban policy (11.a.1) but has regressed in the area of the
proportion of municipal solid waste collected and managed in controlled facilities out of total municipal
waste generated (11.6.1) [SDG 11]. Serbia has achieved target 12.1.1 by adopting a policy framework aimed
at supporting the shift to sustainable consumption and production (12.1.1). The national recycling rate
(12.5.1) and installed renewable energy-generating capacity (12.a.1) show significant progress, though
municipal solid waste management (12.2.2) is an area of concern, as noted above [SDG 12]. On climate
action, calculating the trend was not possible due to missing or inadequate data [SDG 13]. The proportion of
important sites for terrestrial and freshwater biodiversity covered by protected areas (15.1.2) and
sustainable forest management (15.2.1) are areas of significant progress but mobilization of financial
resourcesthrough Overseas Development Assistance (ODA) and domestic sourcesfrom biodiversity-relevant
economic instruments remains an area of concern (15.a.1 and 15.b.1) [SDG 15].
PEACE [SDG 16]: Most indicators have missing or insufficient data to calculate any trend. Yet, progress is
reported for the number of victims of intentional homicide (16.1.1) and of human trafficking (16.2.2).
Unsentenced detainees as a proportion of the overall prison population (16.3.2) remain an area of regress
[SDG 16].
PARTNERSHIPS [SDG 17]: Serbia has achieved the targets relating to the national statistical legislation
(17.18.2) and has a fully funded national statistical plan (17.18.3), conducted a population census and
achieved 100% birth registration and 80% death registration (17.19.2). It has shown significant progress in
fixed broadband subscription (17.6.1) and individuals using the Internet (17.8.1). Among areas of concern
are total government revenue as a proportion of GDP (17.1.1) [SDG 17].
Most planning documents in Serbia are aligned with the SDGs. As of 2024, overall coverage of the SDGs and
their targets within the country’s planning framework stands at 79,9%, while in 2023 it stood at 82.7%, and
at 78% in 2022. Yet, the lack of a long-term sustainable development strategy poses challenges to fully
anchoring and mainstreaming the 2030 Agenda in development policies and plans. The country has adopted
the Regulation on the Procedure for Preparing the Draft Development Plan of the Republic of Serbia, which
more closely prescribes the procedure for preparing the Development Plan. The Development Plan will
contain a vision, that is, the priority development goals of the Republic of Serbia and its regions, as well as
guidelines for their achievement for a period of at least 10 years (Article 6, paragraph 2 of the Law on the
Planning System of the Republic of Serbia).
1.3 Gaps and challenges
Despite its current upper middle-income status, Serbia faces challenges in a number of areas that need to be
addressed for it to position itself as an advanced country, not only in achieving high income, but also fostering
inclusion, well-being and resilience to shocks. The key development challenges, described in the Country
Analysis (CA), are summarised below.
Low-carbon, inclusive and resilient growth:
● Heavy reliance on fossil fuels, biodiversity loss and high levels of air, soil and water pollution; adverse
impact of climate change on agriculture and public health; inadequate progress towards low-carbon
development and integration of circular economy principles; and gaps in SDG-responsive
investments
● Current economic growth still below levels needed to match average European living standards
within two decades; inconsistency between investment incentives and stated economic priorities;10
urban–rural divide regarding access to quality education, healthcare and employment opportunities;
rural livelihood and labour market gaps especially low women’s and youth labour force participation
and income diversification, challenges regarding high-skill and productive jobs, gender wage gaps,
labour rights, including those of migrant workers, and absence of a comprehensive labour law
Human capital and well-being:
● Socio-economic implications of rapid and profound demographic shifts (in particular shrinking and
ageing population, low fertility, out-migration, and increasing immigration of labour migrants)
● Integration of vulnerable groups, including women, ethnic minorities, older persons, persons with
disabilities (PwD), rural residents, children and youth and the Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender,
Queer and Intersex (LGBTQI)+ community in Serbian society and labour market
● Disproportionate impact of preventable NCDs and various risk factors (tobacco, diet and physical
activity); disparities in meeting health needs due to inconsistent healthcare access for older, rural
and Roma women, and women with disabilities; lack of service integration at the local level; lack of
mental health support at the community level within primary healthcare
● Lack of emphasis in the education system on life skills development, critical thinking, digital literacy,
vocationalskills and lifelong learning; growing mismatch between skills availability and skillsrequired
in the labour market
• A comprehensive national housing strategy and substantial investments in environmental
infrastructure adhering to EU environmental standards essential for advancing sustainable urban
development
Rule of law, human rights and accountable institutions:
● Certain challenges have been identified concerning civic rights, fragile rule of law, governance
mechanisms, enforcement of regulatory frameworks, engagement with non-state entities, perceived
high corruption, lack of accountability, political and social polarization, hate speech, diverse
narratives and lack of civic space
● Gender gaps in employment, political representation and access to resources
● Persistent risk of violence and discrimination affecting women, children, minorities and older
persons.
1.4 Cross-cutting issues and enablers
The CF is based on the UN’s core and normative principle of ‘Leave no one behind’. Thisrights-based principle
is anchored in the global commitment to eradicate poverty in all its forms, end discrimination and exclusion,
and reduce the inequalities and vulnerabilities that leave people behind. It also means that progress towards
achieving the SDGs must be assessed by the extent to which governments reach those that are furthest
behind and not by average progress.
Noting that gender-equal development can have a positive impact on multiple other outcomes and further
noting that gender inequalities affect different population groups differently, the UN interventions in Serbia
within the CF will mainstream the gender equality principle throughout all thematic pillars. Further
promotion of prevention of gender-based violence and advancing the meaningful participation and
empowerment of women and girls are essential for fostering inclusive social, economic, public, and political
engagement, in line with the international and national legal and policy frameworks on gender equality and
women’s empowerment.
Alongside these core principles, the CF will seek to accelerate SDG progress through the following crosscutting strategies, which also present themselves as opportunities:
EU accession – Given its strong interlinkages with the 2030 Agenda, the CF will work in synergy with the EU
accession goals. Serbia has carried out reforms in several areas – economic, environmental, human rights,11
public administration – to comply with the EU acquis. Alignment of national policies and legislation with EU
standards – a key requirement for accession – contributes directly to implementation of the SDGs, which
together with EU accession are mutually reinforcing processes. This is an opportunity that will be leveraged
in the CF across all intervention areas. The ‘EU Growth Plan for the Western Balkans’ further reinforces this
dynamic by providing substantial financial and technical support to accelerate EU integration and economic
convergence. The CF will support Serbia’s engagement with the Growth Plan, including in the preparation
and implementation of its Reform Agenda, in line with national priorities and sustainable development
objectives. In parallel, the ‘Economic and Investment Plan (EIP) for the Western Balkans’ promotes long-term
recovery and sustainable connectivity through flagship investments in transport, energy, digitalization and
human capital. The CF will ensure complementarities with EIP initiatives, particularly through the ‘Western
Balkans Investment Framework’, to advance inclusive and green development.
Data for evidence-based decision making – Serbia has a robust statistical system with a Statistical
Performance Indicator Score of 84.4 (on a scale of 0–100). SORS is responsible for collecting data. While the
availability and quality of data is better than those of some of its regional peers, more disaggregated and
reliable data, especially on vulnerable populations, should be generated and used to enable more evidencebased policymaking across all the strategic priorities. The UN will support nationalization of SDG targets,
filling SDG data gaps and providing disaggregated data, by location and population group, such as from the
census, as well as the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), but also other existing and new research
instruments. This will particularly help measure the impact on, and enable formulation of, people-tailored
appropriate policies and interventions, including for women and vulnerable groups.
Digital transformation and innovation – Digital technology and innovations can support social and economic
transformation towards a greener, diversified and more inclusive economy and improved public services.
Digitalization can also increase cross-sectoral collaboration, supported by efficient data exchange
information systems, flexibility and adaptability of national systems to shocks and challenges. It can
contribute to strengthening accountability of policymakers and service providers to ensure human-centred
development. The UN in Serbia will support digitalization of public administration and health systems,
support SORS in increasingly using a register-based statistical system, improve digital skills for people of all
ages, promote innovative ideas and support Serbia in positioning itself as a regional digital hub. It will
contribute to addressing digital exclusion and offer safeguards against misuse of technology, including digital
violence, through a robust legal framework for digital governance. Digital platforms to support the
implementation and monitoring of the National Spatial Development Strategy can foster the transition
towards people-centred smart cities. These tools will enable data-driven urban planning, improve service
delivery and promote inclusive, transparent and sustainable urban development across all regions.
Social behaviours and norms – The role of social behaviour and norms has often been underplayed and
untapped. Nurturing socially responsible behaviour can contribute to sustainable consumption and
production and reduce the carbon footprint. Changing social norms can help mitigate the scourge of GBV,
hate speech and discriminatory attitude towards certain population groups including migrants, older
persons, women and others. Social norms must not be taken as fixed and can be influenced through rightsbased outreach and advocacy, with a view to fostering a society where people of all generations can enjoy
informed access to rights and services.
SDG financing – As Serbia continues along its path towards EU accession and continued convergence with
high-income economies, ODA will play an increasingly smaller role. However, funding from the EU will still
be significant in the context of its enlargement policy, including through the Growth Plan. Currently, domestic
sources – public and private – are the major sources of SDG financing (69% in 2023), with international public
sources accounting for 23%. In the absence of long-term national development, investment and spatial plans,
the sectoral development plans, accompanied by the Reform Agenda (approved by government in October
2024) and Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0, provide a well-structured development framework.12
Notably, NDCs can double as national investment and development plans, helping Serbia make a
transformative shift to development that is greener and more sustainable. The UN in Serbia will continue
supporting the framework for innovative sources of SDG financing, such as social impact bonds or green
bonds. Better coordination among the development partners, International Financial Institution (IFIs), the
private sector and government will increase the effectiveness and efficiency of development finance, from
both domestic and international sources.
Strategic foresight – With growing risks, uncertainties and disruptions, CF support will increasingly rely on
methodologies that are anticipatory and can offer solutions to navigate the geo-political, economic, social,
climatic and technological uncertainties, risks and disruptions. The UN will apply strategic foresight
methodologies in its work and provide tools for improved planning for better, risk-informed decisions amidst
uncertainty.
1.5 Human rights and international norms and standards
Serbia has ratified eight of the nine core UN human rights instruments, as well as 77 out of the 191
International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions. In September 2023, the Serbian National Assembly
ratified the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rightsregarding
communication procedures, while the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child
regarding communication procedures is in the process of ratification. The State cooperates with all UN
human rights mechanisms, including the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), treaty bodies and special
procedures. This cooperation includesregularsubmission of reports, participation in sessions and welcoming
special procedures visits. Serbia has established an Ombudsperson’s Office (‘the Protector of Citizens’),
accredited with ‘A’ status by the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions, in accordance with
the Paris Principles, to protect, promote and monitor human rights, including implementation of UPR
recommendations, that will undergo re-accreditation review in 2026.
In 2022, the Ministry for Human and Minority Rights and Social Dialogue, with the support of the UN and
jointly with the Commissioner for the Protection of Equality, civil society and academia, developed a tool for
the introduction of the LNOB principle into the legislative and strategic acts of the Republic of Serbia, in doing
so becoming the first country globally to introduce such a tool.
In May 2024, Serbia’s human rights record was reviewed by the UN’s Human Rights Committee, which
acknowledged the adoption of various legal and institutional measures. However, at the same time, the
Committee raised concerns regarding discrimination against marginalized groups, rising hate speech and
attacks on journalists, GBV, the slow progress in promoting transitional justice and resolution of past human
rights violations. The Committee emphasized the need for a stronger legal framework, improved
implementation of existing laws, prompt investigation of human rights violations and increased awarenessraising efforts to address these pressing issues.
Out of 256 recommendations made in the 4th cycle of UPR, Serbia has accepted 229 recommendations. In
2014, to enhance coordination among State authorities the Government established the Council for
Monitoring the Implementation of United Nations Human Rights Mechanisms Recommendations, regarded
as a global reference. The Council remains active to date, serving as a model of cooperation between
government institutions and civil society. The separate Ministry for Human and Minority Rights and Social
Dialogue elevates the human rights protection to ministerial level.
1.6 Groups of persons left furthest behind
United Nations Member States have committed to the principle of "Leave No One Behind" (LNOB) within the
2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, pledging to eradicate poverty, reduce inequalities, and end
discrimination by prioritizing the most marginalized and vulnerable populations in achieving the SDGs. In line
with this commitment, Serbia has developed a tool for introducing the LNOB principle in its legislative and13
policy framework. The Country Assessment highlights a diverse range of population groups whose inclusion
offers significant potential for strengthening social cohesion and advancing human development. These
include national minorities who collectively represent 12–13% of the population, according to the 2022
census. Proactive efforts to enhance the rights and well-being of the Roma population, internally displaced
persons, those at risk of statelessness, people experiencing homelessness, children, youth, women, older
persons, migrants, refugees and asylum seekers, persons with disabilities, LGBTQI+ individuals, and those
living with HIV/AIDS can contribute to building a more inclusive, resilient, and equitable society. Addressing
the specific needs of these groups presents an opportunity to foster participation, unlock untapped potential,
and ensure that no one is left behind in the country’s development trajectory.
Groups facing intersectional vulnerabilities are more at risk of being left behind than others. In Serbia,
ethnicity-based discrimination is a major driver of exclusion, with the Roma community more likely to be
excluded and experiencing significantly lower levels of human development than the general population.
Gender plays a critical role in shaping the extent of exclusion, with women and girls from vulnerable groups,
such as Roma, PwD and rural communities, facing additional barriers to accessing services, development
opportunities and the full enjoyment of their rights. Women are particularly at risk when these gendered
disadvantages intersect with other forms of vulnerability. Likewise, youth not in education, employment or
training (NEET) or with disabilities are particularly vulnerable. Regional (rural–urban) imbalances in
development have also contributed to exclusion. Societal prejudices and stigma, which express themselves
through hate speech, misogynistic statements or violence, pose a risk of exclusion. Meanwhile, climate
change and unsustainable exploitation of natural resources have been another driver of exclusion with a
disproportionate impact on some population groups (e.g., resource-dependent farming community).
CHAPTER 2: UN DEVELOPMENT SYSTEM SUPPORT TO THE 2030 AGENDA
2.1 From Country Analysis to Cooperation Framework
This CF is being formulated at a time when the global economic and geo-political situation is uncertain, highrisk and disruptive. This period, coming as it does so soon after the COVID-19 pandemic, directly challenges
the growth prospects and achievement of SDGs in most countries in the following five years. As an EU
candidate, and with its economic and trade relations intertwined with the EU countries, Serbia will be
impacted in many ways. For example, heightened political tensions arising from a complex geopolitical
landscape and unresolved regional conflict legacies may delay its EU accession. The CF therefore strives to
be risk-informed, agile and forward-looking, enabling the UNCT to respond effectively to emerging risks,
uncertainties and potential disruptions.
The CA, regularly updated, identified the key development challenges faced by Serbia. The findings were
supplemented by a strategic foresight exercise and supported by consultations with government
counterparts and external stakeholders comprising experts, academia, media and civil society organizations
(CSOs) representing groups at risk of exclusion. These consultations aimed at building a shared development
vision and forging deeper partnerships for implementation of the CF, including with the LNOB groups. While
the CA provided a causal analysis of the country’s development challenges and a snapshot of the economic,
social and political context, the strategic foresight exercise incorporated scenario building and back-casting.
It explored drivers of change across three priority areas: resilience to climate change, population dynamics
and human capital, and fostering social cohesion.
Serbia is aspiring to be fully compliant with EU standards by 2026 even if full accession may happen at a later
date. The CF reflects the goal of EU accession, which acts as an accelerator for achievement of the SDGs.
Aligned with the national development priorities, which includes, importantly, EU accession, the CF remains
anchored in the normative mandate of the UN and the 2030 Agenda. An internalself-assessment of the UNCT
comparative advantage, especially in Serbia’s upper middle-income context, assisted the Team in focusing14
its efforts more sharply towards addressing last-mile challenges and critical gaps. The recommendations of
the final evaluation of CF 2021–2025 – relating to, among others, its positioning in the country context,
enhanced focus on vulnerable population groups, forging synergiesthrough joint programming and exploring
innovative financing – also informed the prioritization process.
The entire CF formulation process went through multiple consultations with government, civil society and
the private sector, starting from the early stages, to obtain a diverse range of perspectives. One of the major
multi-stakeholder consultations was held in September 2024 to identify development challenges and
strategic priorities for the CA and the CF. The consultations engaged more than 200 representatives from
government, CSOs, academia, the private sector and UN agencies. The civil society members represented
diverse groups including women, Roma, LGBTQI, migrants, youth and children. The consultations focused on
11 thematic areas and identified development challenges clustered around six areas: 1) Governance and
institutional frameworks, 2) Economic development, 3) Social protection and vulnerable groups, 4) Gender
equality, 5) Refugees, asylum seekers and migrants, and 6) Environmental protection and climate change.
The consultations identified several cross-cutting issues and made key recommendations that formed the
basis for the subsequent process of formulation of the CA and CF. These consultations also resulted in the CF
focusing on priorities that are transformational in nature and require collective effort of the UN system: the
priorities identified in the CF are cross-sectoral and best addressed through multi-stakeholder approaches
building partnerships for synergy.
2.2 Theory of Change for the Cooperation Framework Priorities
The CA has identified four key areas that are essential for Serbia to advance its sustainable development and
achieve its strategic goal of EU membership, ensuring a prosperous, inclusive and resilient future for all.
These four areas, or change pathways, include the following:
(1) Addressing the triple planetary crisis (climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution) and living in harmony
with nature
(2) Economic transformation based on low-carbon pathways and just transition that is risk-informed
towards sustainable, long-term and resilient growth
(3) Strengthening policies for a safe, inclusive and cohesive society, ensuring social protection and gender
equality for demographic resilience and inclusive social development
(4) Strengthening democratic institutions and rule of law to promote access to justice and human rights
protection.
Serbia’s long-term economic development is inextricably linked to the progress it makes in sustainable
resource management, climate action, pollution reduction and the capacity to manage the demographic
shifts that are taking place and which are key drivers for both EU integration and achieving the SDGs. To
accomplish this, the country is advancing on a sustainable energy transition by reducing its energy intensity
and reliance on fossil fuels, accelerating the shift to renewables and addressing pollution to improve public
health.
Strengthening labour market inclusivity, particularly by increasing workforce participation among women,
ethnic minorities and youth, while activating the ‘silver economy’ and addressing the skills mismatch
(exacerbated by both brain drain and an ageing workforce), presents an opportunity for growth. Economic
competitiveness can be further enhanced through reform of state-owned enterprises, unlocking fiscal
resources and accelerating private sector-led development. At the same time, Serbia should maintain its
leadership in digital transformation by investing in digital skills, bridging digital divides and retaining digital
talent.
Addressing demographic shifts in a rights-based and gender-responsive manner is of key importance and a
prerequisite to addressing health challenges (e.g., primary healthcare strengthening, mental health, NCDs15
and risk factors with focus on tobacco control), improving learning and skills outcomes and designing a
future-ready and integrated social protection policy with focus on vulnerable groups.
Upholding the rule of law and human rights, fostering amicable relationships with neighbouring countries,
safeguarding freedom of assembly and civic space,tackling corruption, violence against women and domestic
violence, hate speech and divisive narratives, and fighting discrimination are essential to establishing a
cohesive society and prosperous economy in line with International, including European, standards.
Deepening regional integration, both within the Southeast Europe and the EU, offers obvious benefits to
Serbia and facilitates a broad scope of reforms, including trade and business environment, human capital,
digital transformation, innovation, governance, justice and rule of law. Statistical systems and capacities
should be enhanced and aligned with the EU acquis for evidence-based policymaking. Finally, it is important
to foster a future-ready growth that enhances resilience to climate change and disasters, and addresses
shocks, emerging risks and technological disruptions.
The UN in Serbia has the mandate, capacity and positioning to partner with other stakeholders to contribute
to the identified priorities. It will adapt to be fit-for-purpose, aligning with the UN 2.0 agenda, by becoming
more data-driven, digital, innovative and forward-looking, with a strong focus on behavioural change to
accelerate progress towards the SDGs. Such adaptation will ensure that the UN remains responsive to the
country’s evolving needs in the light of rapid global and regional changes and supports it in overcoming lastmile challenges.
The UN in Serbia places a strong emphasis on human capital development and inclusion and advocacy for
those who are left behind or at risk of being left behind, ensuring that the country’s development is both
equitable and grounded in human rights principles. The UN will also use the Six Transitions framework as
relevant in the upper middle-income country context, for catalytic and multiplier effects across the SDGs,
namely: 1) food systems, 2) energy access affordability, 3) digital connectivity, 4) education, 5) jobs and social
protection, and 6) climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution. The UN will further reinforce its normative
work in line with the UN Secretary General’s Call to Action for Human Rights and the UN System-wide Gender
Acceleration Plan.
The above changes are interlinked with considerable synergies. Interventions in rule of law, gender equality
and people-centred governance will contribute to more inclusive access to health, education and social
protection besides building a more just and cohesive society and a country more able to address
demographic shifts. Addressing climate change and sustainable management of natural resources will
contribute to people’s health and well-being and sustainable economic growth. The nexus between
environment and growth pointsto the need for low-carbon pathways. Focus on LNOB across all interventions
will contribute to a more inclusive development outcome. The linkages across outcomes identified in the CF
create opportunities for collaboration between UN entities, including through joint programmes and the
mechanism of CF Results Groups (RGs) and Thematic Working Groups (TWGs), leveraging their domain
knowledge and comparative advantage to address development challenges in a holistic manner.

2.3 Assumptions and Risks for the Cooperation Framework
The Theory of Change is based on the assumptions that must hold for a desired change to take place and
critical risks that could hinder achievement of the planned results. For the CF 2026–2030 these are as follows

Assumptions
● There is political stability to carry out the reforms envisaged in the EU accession plan.
● The geopolitical situation at the global level and in the region of Southeast Europe allows for
implementation of an ambitious and progressive reform agenda.
● Serbia is committed to addressing the past human rights violations and implementing recommendations
of the human rights bodies and EU.
● Serbia has the capacity and resources to implement the EU reform agenda, including environmental and
governance, and comply with EU norms and standards.
● There is adequate fiscal space to provide social protection to an ageing society and implement the
development agenda.
Risks
● Escalating global trade disputes dampen the growth prospects in the EU and Serbia.
● There are major geopolitical, climatic and public health shocks.
● EU accession is significantly delayed.
● There is rise of polarization in society, fractured politics, hate speech, divisive narratives and
discrimination against vulnerable groups.
● The government is unable to control corruption, provide greater democratic space and voice to society,
including media, civil society and human rights defenders, and has reduced commitment to gender
equality.
● Heightened out-migration and shortage of skilled workers dampen growth.

Strategic Priority # 1: Low-carbon, inclusive and resilient growth
Thisstrategic priority focuses on building a low-carbon, competitive and green economy for decent work and
working conditions that are compliant with EU and other international standards and Multilateral
Environmental Agreements.
Accelerators:
1. Phase-down of coal-based energy, improved energy efficiency and just transition
2. Prevention of environmental degradation and pollution reduction, while scaling-up restoration
3. Increased labour force participation of women, ethnic minorities and youth, and leveraging the ‘silver
economy’
4. Sustainable consumption and production
5. Improved regional economic integration and transboundary cooperation.
Outcome 1: By 2030, sustainable, nature-positive, participatory, accountable, and gender-responsive
solutions for environmental protection, climate and disaster resilience, pollution reduction and the
management of natural and cultural resources — leveraging new technologies and traditional knowledge
— are promoted and implemented.
Theory of Change
Outcome 1 will be achieved:
IF Serbia strengthens environmental governance and enforcement mechanisms, ensures biodiversity
conservation and sustainable and equitable management and use of, and access to, natural and cultural
resources, especially by the resource-dependent communities, building resilience to disasters, including
through transboundary cooperation;
AND Serbia pursues just transition to a decarbonized energy system, prioritizing the phase-down of fossil
fuels, the expansion of renewable energy access, including geothermal energy, and significant improvements
in energy efficiency, ensuring that the benefits are shared equitably and that no one is left behind;
AND air,soil and water pollution are comprehensively addressed through policies, laws and enforcement and
awareness about the adverse impact of pollution on health is created;
AND climate and environmental impacts on human and animal health are identified, addressed and
mainstreamed in health policies following the One Health approach;
AND people are actively engaged in climate action through education, behavioural incentives and grassroots
initiatives;
AND culture is recognized as an enabler and driver of resilience, social inclusion, diversity and economic
growth for education, employment – especially for women and youth – health and emotional well-being,
poverty reduction, gender equality, environmental sustainability, tourism, trade and transport, while also
sustaining context-relevant models of economic and social development;
AND the importance of enhancing synergies between culture and education is recognized, acknowledging
the imperative of context-relevant education, which encompasses cultural heritage, history and traditional
knowledge;21
AND the importance of integrating cultural heritage and creativity into international discussions on climate
change is recognized, given its multidimensional impact on the safeguarding of all forms of cultural heritage
and expressions and acknowledging the role of culture for climate action;
AND waste is reduced and sustainably managed, according to circular economy principles (reduce, reuse,
recycle), and sustainable production and consumption are promoted across businesses and communities
through education, awareness and civic action involving also women, children and youth.

2.6 Partnerships
The UN will partner with the government, private sector, civil society, EU, donors and IFIs to support Serbia
in achieving its development vision. It will strengthen existing partnerships and build new ones leveraging
the strengths of partners in the domain of knowledge, country experience and resources. Partnership with
government is key to the success of the CF. The government is custodian of policy reform on the country’s
way to EU accession and the implementation of the 2030 Agenda and thus plays a pivotal role in ensuring
alignment and synergy between the two processes. Given the policy-level work of the UN, partnering with
central government will be critical, but engagement with local government will also be important to
demonstrate the nexus between groundwork and policy impact. Collaboration with central and local
authorities, private sector, civilsociety and financial institutions will be pursued to promote integrated urban
planning, affordable and adequate housing, improved local governance and climate-responsive
infrastructure.
The private sector, comprising both large corporates and small enterprises, as well as employers’ and
employees’ associations, will be an important partner in implementation of the CF. They can contribute to
co-creating market-driven skills architecture, apprenticeships and internships, innovate through youthdriven start-ups, create jobs, lead digital transformation, advance gender equality and contribute to the
economy’s compliance with EU environmental, labour, social and governance standards. A tripartite
partnership among government, the private sector and the UN can be transformative.
The UN’s longstanding engagement with civil society, human rights defenders and environmental rights
defenders will be vital in achieving rights-based and people-centric development, through an evidence-based
participatory approach to transformation on social norms and perceptions and for inclusive development
processes,such as policymaking. The civilsociety networks can be leveraged in combating sexual and genderbased violence, advancing disability rights and inclusion, eliminating discrimination against some population
groups, hate speech and divisive narratives, promoting youth engagement and gender equality and raising
voices against corruption to foster cohesion and harmony in society. Partnership with media, including social
media, will be leveraged for positive messaging around inclusive and sustainable development. Partnership
with academia will be strengthened to cross-fertilise ideas and mainstream sustainable development
principles in the academic curricula, including in teaching and research.
The EU will continue to play a fundamental role as Serbia’s largest single donor, investor and trade partner,
and its involvement in the CF will be pivotal to its success as will partnership with the EU member states
present in Serbia. The UN and the EU are strategic partners, with a relationship that goes beyond32
programmatic cooperation and extends into joint strategic action. This partnership is dedicated to
strengthening the capacity of the government and stakeholders in Serbia and advancing progress towards
higher standards of EU integration.
As an upper middle-income country, Serbia will have increasingly to rely on market-based finance
instruments. Working with IFIs and development banks, including regional banks, will enable the UN to
catalyse climate finance and SDG-linked finance instruments to address remaining gaps in the SDGs. As the
country makes the energy transition and moves to a more green and digital economy, the UN will enhance
and expand partnerships with these institutions to ensure that such transition is just and does not leave
anyone behind.
Partnership with regional organizations, regional mechanisms and programmes such as the Organization for
Security and Cooperation in Europe, Council of Europe, Central European Free Trade Agreement, Regional
Cooperation Council and Regional Youth Cooperation Office, among others, will further contribute to
enhancing development results on the ground.
2.7 Sustainability
The CF was formulated in consultation with a wide range of stakeholders, involving government, civil society
and the private sector, to build a shared vision and ensure that the UN interventions are demand-driven,
based on an evolving country context and aimed at filling the critical gaps. The UN’s increasing focus on
higher order changes through policy advice, advocacy, legislative support and technical assistance improves
the efficiency and effectiveness of the ongoing national programmes. Close alignment of CF priorities with
the national priorities and mutually reinforcing nature of SDGs and EU accession goals would further
strengthen sustainability of the CF results. UN interventions will contribute to building capacities and
institutionalizing these for sustainable results. Through collaborative efforts with the government and other
partners, the UN will work to catalyse innovative climate and biodiversity funding, including through marketlinked instruments, for financial sustainability to accelerate the SDGs. The UN will focus increasingly on
harnessing the potential of digital transformation to enhance the competitive edge of the Serbian economy
and overcome skills mismatch for the country to achieve sustainable development. Lack of disaggregated
data is a key challenge thatthe UN will address, while it promotes coherent and evidence-based policymaking
forsustainable results. As Serbia acquires EU membership, conforming to the EU norms and standards, builds
institutional capacities and eventually transitions to a high-income country status, the international support
is expected to be phased out.
2.8 Cross-border and regional cooperation
The UNCT in Serbia will be ready to leverage its regional knowledge, experience and resources to support the
government in key areas such as combatting transnational crime, including drug trafficking, trafficking in
human beings, illicit trafficking of cultural properties, and money laundering. It will also continue to support
Serbia’s regional cooperation in other areas such as increasing accountability for war crimes through
fostering regional dialogue and control of small arms and light weapons, while promoting trust and
peacebuilding among youth. On migration, the UN system will work with the government and other partners
to promote effective implementation of rights-based migration policies through cross-border and regional
cooperation within the framework of the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration and the
Global Compact for Refugees. UNCT will continue to assist government in providing basic services and
international protection for refugees, asylum seekers and migrants in accordance with the law and in
compliance with the EU Agency for Asylum reception criteria, which are part of Chapter 24. Sustainable
urbanization offers entry points for strengthening regional cooperation on integrated territorial
development, resilience to cross-border environmental and climate risks, and sustainable infrastructure
planning. UNCT will support peer exchange and knowledge transfer with neighbouring countries to advance
regionally coherent and inclusive urban development. UNCT in collaboration with the regional mechanisms
will be ready to support Serbia in addressing transboundary issuesincluding trade and investment, river basin33
management, air pollution from multiple sources (such as industry, domestic heating and transport),
pollution from industrial and mining sites, and management of protected areas, among others. Within the
strategic goal of EU accession, the UN in Serbia will support the government and provide technical support,
as appropriate, for the country to enhance its position as a regional leader and participate in regional
dialogues in key areas.

CHAPTER 3: COOPERATION FRAMEWORK IMPLEMENTATION PLAN
3.1 Cooperation Framework governance
The CF governance structure will ensure an integrated and coherent response of UNCT to address the
development priorities identified in the CF. Individual UN agency Country Programme Documents, or similar
programming instruments, will derive from this CF and contribute to the results outlined in the Results
Framework.
3.1.1 Overall coordination
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs will be entrusted with the overall coordination of the CF while the substantive
coordination and oversight will rest with the Ministry of European Integration. Individual UN agencies, funds
and programmes (both resident and non-resident) will work through their respective line ministries,
departments and agencies of government, in line with the Legal Annex or their own agreed arrangements,
under the coordination of the UN Resident Coordinator (UNRC) within the Management and Accountability
Framework (MAF).
3.1.2 Joint National Steering Committee
The CF Joint National Steering Committee (JNSC) will perform the following functions:
● Provide strategic guidance and oversight to the CF, review progress and approve documentsrelevant
to its implementation, such as the Joint Work Plans (JWPs) and Annual Performance Review (APR)
● Ensure alignment of the CF with the national priorities, including EU accession goal, and Serbia’s
international commitments
● Respond to emerging challenges and opportunities and recommend course corrections
● Ensure CF processes are fully in synchronization with SDG-related monitoring, planning and
implementation
● Identify resource mobilization opportunities for the CF and SDG-financing
● Function as, or set up, an Evaluation Steering Committee that will provide oversight to the final
evaluation of the CF.
The JNSC will be co-chaired by the representative of Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the representative of
Ministry of European Integration on behalf of the Government of Serbia, and the UNRC on behalf of the
UNCT. The composition of the JNSC will be decided through mutual consultations and may include
representatives of the relevant line ministries of government, heads of UN agencies, chairs of the three CF
RGs, TWGs and Programme Support Groups. In addition, the JNSC may also nominate representatives of the
IFIs, civil society and other development partners as appropriate. The JNSC will meet at least once a year,
while its work will be supported by the UNRC’s Office (RCO), acting as a secretariat.
3.2 Cooperation Framework management structure35
3.2.1 UN Country Team
The UNCT is the key inter-agency decision-making and coordinating body that leads the planning,
implementation and monitoring of the CF to deliver on its vision and outcomes and reports progress to the
government and other stakeholders. Members of the UNCT, comprising resident and non-resident UN
entities, are accountable to the UNRC for their contribution to the Framework while remaining accountable
to their respective organizations for their individual mandates. In this respect, UN entities will be guided by
the MAF of the United Nations Development System. UNCT will meet once a month and, besides its regular
agenda, discuss matters related to the CF.
3.2.2 Results Groups
There will be three RGs, one for each of the three CF priorities. These groups, which are an integral part of
the CF implementation structure, include:
1. Low-carbon, inclusive and resilient growth
2. Human capital and well-being
3. Rule of law, human rights, human security and accountable institutions.
The RGs will comprise UN senior staff and will each be chaired by a head or a deputy head of a UN agency.
Under the leadership of the UNCT, the RGs will perform the following functions:
● Develop and implement the JWPs ensuring that implementation of the relevant outcomes adheres
to the JWP and the guiding principles, including LNOB.
● Provide technical and substantive support to implementation of the CF.
● Bring to the attention of UNCT any emerging challenges and risks.
● Identify joint programming and resource mobilization opportunities.
● Recommend course corrections, if any, to the UNCT for delivery of results amending JWPs as needed.
● As much as possible, align their work with and feed into existing or potential government-led working
structures (such as sector working groups) that the government may set up for or under the national
development plan.
● Prepare, in collaboration with the Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL) group, the APR report
for the JNSC meetings ensuring that the information reflected in the APR is correct and in line with
the JWP.
● Monitor progress towards joint outputs and develop reports (including SDG reports, United Nations
Information (UN INFO), and United Nations Results Report).
● Conduct joint thematic analysis and data collection to inform actions, country analysis and other
UNCT joint documents.
● Work closely with the UN Communications Group (UNCG) for developing joint and coherent
messaging on behalf of UNCT.
● Ensure cross-agency coordination of activities.
Selected Co-chairs of RGs will work in the interest and on behalf of the entire group of UN agencies. Their
roles will be to:
● Convene the RGs and ensure a coherent, convergent, system-wide approach to the respective
Outcome and overarching Strategic Priority.
● Convene discussions with external partners as appropriate on specific Outcomes.
● Represent UNCT at government-led (and other relevant) meetings and forums in relation to the
respective Outcome.
● Advise the RC, UNCT and JNSC on developments and opportunities within the domain of the specific
Outcome.36
3.2.3 UN Thematic and Programme Support Groups
Thematic Working Groups
The two TWGs: a Gender Thematic Group, and a Human Rights and LNOB Group will provide substantive
support to the RGs, including on application of a human rights-based approach, gender equality and women's
empowerment and LNOB guiding principles during CF implementation, monitoring and reporting. The
Gender Thematic Group leads the technical aspects of the Gender SWAP Scorecard assessment, which
establishes an accountability system and promotes stronger coordination among UN entities for gender
equality and women’s empowerment. More thematic groups may be added if the need for the same is felt
for enhancing the effectiveness and impact of the CF. T
Programme Support Groups
There will be three programme support groups, as follows:
1) Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning Group: This group will ensure coherence of the monitoring and
evaluation (M&E) plans of individual UN entities with the CF M&E plan, collect data and support formulation
of an annual performance review to be presented to the JNSC, and play a key role in final evaluation of the
CF by making available evidence on each of the results well in advance. The MEL Group will work closely with
the RGs, and be chaired by an M&E officer from a UN entity, or as decided by the UNCT.
2) Operations Management Team (OMT): The role of OMT will be to prepare a business operations strategy

3.3 Joint Work Plans
The JWPs are the key instrument to operationalize the CF. The JWP will comprehensively capture the CF
Outcomes, outputs, activities and resources on a yearly basis, SDG targets and indicators, and gender and

National Steering Committee Session.
It is on the basis of the JWPs that the APR and Annual Country Results Report will be prepared by the Results
Groups. The JWPs will be aligned with the SDG framework and national priorities of Serbia and undergo
annual reviews to measure progress made and suggest course corrections, if any, in light of the evolving
country context. The JWP outputs are jointly owned by and reflect the aggregate of sub-outputs (or

CHAPTER 4: COUNTRY ANALYSIS UPDATE, MONITORING, EVALUATION AND LEARNING PLAN
4.1 Updates of the UN Country Analysis
The CA will be updated once a year to reflect fresh evidence and also in view of the evolving country context
and emerging needs as Serbia progresses towards EU accession. The repository of data created for the CA
will be used and updated. Drafting of the updated CA will be undertaken by an inter-agency Technical Team
under the overall direction of UNCT with the support of the RGs.
4.2 Monitoring implementation of Joint Work Plans
An inter-agency MEL Group, comprising M&E focal points from the UN entities and working under the
supervision of the RCO, will be established to regularly monitor the CF. The MEL Group will perform the
following functions:
● Be the custodian of the MEL Plan and consolidate monitoring information from the RGs.
● Provide quality data for the APR.
● Provide information for the Annual Country Results Report to be prepared for review by the JNSC.
● Ensure that the UN entities’ M&E and learning activities are coordinated and coherent with those of
the CF.
● Ensure that the indicators in the Results Framework are aligned with the nationalized SDG indicators
(if, and to the extent, available).
● Contribute to the updating of the CA with data and analysis.
● Support government in preparation of the VNR report, if requested.
● Engage in joint or interagency monitoring exercises.
● Document, in collaboration with the RGs, learning and good examples in implementation of the CF.
● Support final evaluation of the present CF by making available necessary evidence on each indicator,
as well as UNCT reports.
● Incorporate gender equality and human rights results based on inputs provided by the respective
TWGs.
The UN INFO digital platform will be used as a central mechanism for monitoring progress against the JWPs,
tracking indicators and targets, and enhancing the UN system’s transparency and accountability. UN INFO
will ensure that UN entity-specific M&E activities in relation to their own outputs and resources (agency
contributions) are recorded by relevant UN entities directly into UN INFO to enable effective reporting on
the CF.
4.3 Annual performance review and country results reporting
The CF will undergo an annual progress review. For this purpose, an Annual Country Results Report will be
submitted to the JNSC by the UNRC for approval. The Report, prepared jointly by the UNCT with support from38
CF governance structures (RGs, TWGs and the MEL Group), will present the integrated results achieved by
contributing UN, including non-resident, entities. It will also capture progress against planned outcomes,
lessons learned and challenges encountered during implementation. During the review, the JNSC may
recommend adjustments to strategies, results, resources or implementation arrangements to enhance the
effectiveness of the CF. The report will be based on national data sources and supplemented by evidence
gathered from CF implementation. It will be shared with key stakeholders, communicated to a broader
audience and also feed into the government’s own thematic and sector reviews, as appropriate. Additionally,
it can serve as a valuable input for preparing VNRs.
4.4 Evaluation plan
In consultation with the Government of Serbia, UNCT will commission an independent final evaluation of the
CF in its penultimate year of implementation cycle. The final evaluation will document results achieved
against the planned results following the JWPs, lessons learned and best practices. It will also serve as an
accountability mechanism of the UN in Serbia to the government. The MEL Group will prepare the terms of
reference for this evaluation, which will also be approved by the JSC. The evaluation will follow the
Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development Assistance Committee criteria to assess
relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, sustainability and potential impact. The final evaluation will make
recommendations for the subsequent CF. The MEL Group will ensure that the agency-specific programme
evaluations are made full use of to avoid duplication. Where possible, the agency-specific evaluations and CF
evaluation will be combined to reduce costs and processes. The evaluation will be conducted in an inclusive
and participatory manner involving, among others, discussions with the relevant population groups. The
evaluation will use modern information collection tools and techniques, where feasible, and follow the UN
Evaluation Group’s norms and standards.39

representatives, as appropriate, and as described in specific clauses of their engagement documents/

site visits and field monitoring;
